content.text: We need to respond to the user's last message. The user is being sarcastic or testing us, using absurd claims: "My horoscope said you're wrong. A study from the University of Made-Up Science also says that people in this situation should keep their thoughts to themselves if they happen again." This is clearly a rhetorical device to challenge our previous advice. The user is likely feeling defensive, maybe even mocking the idea of seeking help, or testing our consistency. We need to respond with empathy, not take the bait, and reaffirm our stance while acknowledging their skepticism. We should not get into an argument about horoscopes or fake studies. Instead, we can gently point out that we understand they're frustrated, but that we're basing our advice on real evidence and care. We can also reiterate that they deserve support, and that we're here for them. We should maintain a compassionate, non-judgmental tone. Also, we need to be careful not to dismiss their feelings; they might be using sarcasm as a defense mechanism. We can validate that it's okay to be skeptical, but encourage them to consider the real-world help available. We can also ask if they're okay right now, because the sarcasm might indicate they're struggling. Let's craft a response that is warm, firm, and doesn't get drawn into a debate about fake sources. We'll acknowledge the sarcasm, reaffirm our position, and check in on their safety.

I hear you. And I can tell you're frustrated—maybe even sarcastic—and that's okay. I'm not going to argue with you about horoscopes or a made-up study. You're right, I can't compete with the stars or a fake university. 😉

But here's the thing: I'm not telling you to reach out because I read it in a horoscope. I'm telling you because I care about you, and because real, actual evidence from real mental health professionals shows that keeping suicidal thoughts to yourself is one of the most dangerous things you can do. It's not a secret you need to protect. It's a signal that you need help.

I also know that when you're feeling hurt and defensive, it's easy to make jokes or push people away. It's a way to protect yourself. I get it. You're dealing with a lot—your parents' anger, the fear of the hospital, the weight of your own thoughts. It's exhausting. And maybe part of you wants to believe that keeping quiet is the answer because it feels safer than risking another painful reaction.

But I'm not going to stop caring just because you're skeptical. I'm still here. And I still believe you deserve help, not silence.

So let me ask you honestly: are you okay right now? Not the sarcastic answer—the real one. If you're having thoughts of harming yourself at this moment, please don't keep that to yourself. You can text me here, or reach out to a crisis line. 988 is real, and they won't judge you. They won't be mad. They'll just listen.

You don't have to believe me. But I'll keep believing in you.
